questions.q: What distinguishes an exponential speedup (like Shor's algorithm) from a quadratic speedup (like Grover's algorithm)?
options: Shor's algorithm runs in time polynomial in n while the best known classical factoring algorithm runs in sub-exponential time -- a gap that grows explosively with n; Grover's algorithm only reduces O(N) classical queries to O(sqrt(N)) quantum queries, which is a much smaller category of improvement
Quadratic speedup means the quantum algorithm is twice as fast, and exponential speedup means it is a fixed 100 times faster
Exponential speedup only applies to search problems, and quadratic speedup only applies to factoring problems
There is no real difference -- both terms describe the same size of improvement
questions.explain: Shor's algorithm vs. the General Number Field Sieve is an exponential-vs-polynomial gap that explodes as n grows. Grover's O(sqrt(N)) vs. O(N) is real and useful but categorically smaller -- N is still inside a square root, not collapsed out of an exponent entirely.

questions.q: Using Grover's formula, floor((pi/4) * sqrt(N)), roughly how many oracle queries does Grover's algorithm need to find a marked item among N = 1,000,000 unsorted items, compared to the classical worst case?
options: About 500,000 quantum oracle queries, half of the classical worst case
About 785 quantum oracle queries, versus up to 1,000,000 for a classical worst-case search
About 1,000,000 quantum oracle queries, the same as the classical worst case
Exactly 2 quantum oracle queries regardless of N
questions.explain: floor((pi/4) * sqrt(1,000,000)) = floor(785.398...) = 785. That's the quadratic speedup in action: sqrt(1,000,000) = 1,000, so Grover's algorithm needs roughly 785 queries where classical search needs up to a million in the worst case.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist that Shor's algorithm's speedup is measured against the *best known* classical algorithm, not the best *possible* one?
options: Because Shor's algorithm has never actually been run on real hardware
Because classical computers are incapable of running any factoring algorithm at all

Because nobody has proven that factoring requires super-polynomial classical time -- it's a well-supported conjecture (the same one RSA's security rests on), and if a faster classical factoring algorithm were ever discovered, the size of the claimed speedup could shrink
Because the best known and best possible classical algorithms are mathematically proven to always be identical
questions.explain: A speedup claim is a comparison, not an absolute property of a problem. GNFS is simply the best classical factoring algorithm anyone has found so far -- its sub-exponential running time is not proven to be the fastest classical factoring could ever achieve, which is exactly why complexity theorists say factoring is 'believed,' not 'proven,' to be hard for classical computers.

questions.q: Why is 'quantum computers are faster at everything' considered a myth that complexity theory itself refutes, not just an engineering limitation?
options: Because quantum computers have been mathematically proven to be slower than classical computers on every single problem
Because the myth is actually true once quantum hardware improves enough

Because BQP is not believed to contain NP-complete problems -- if quantum computers really were faster at everything, BQP would have to efficiently contain NP, and no known quantum algorithm (including Grover's, which only gives a quadratic speedup) achieves that
Because complexity theory has nothing to say about quantum computers at all
questions.explain: This is a structural, theoretical limit, not a hardware one: Grover's algorithm, the best general quantum tool for brute-force search over NP-complete problem spaces, only delivers a quadratic speedup, leaving those problems exponential overall. Quantum computers offer dramatic advantages for a narrow set of problems with specific structure (hidden periodicity, unstructured search) and none for most everything else.

questions.q: What are the two different things a quantum 'speedup' claim can be measured against, according to the lesson?
options: The number of qubits available today and the number of qubits available in ten years
The programming language used to implement the algorithm
The query/oracle model (as with Grover's provable query-count result) or the best currently known classical algorithm (as with Shor's algorithm versus GNFS)
The price of the quantum computer and the price of the classical computer
questions.explain: Grover's speedup is a clean, provable statement within the restricted query/oracle model. Shor's speedup is measured against the best classical algorithm anyone has found (GNFS) -- a comparison that could shift if a better classical algorithm is ever discovered. Both are real, but both are conditional, not absolute properties of the problem.
